title: The Horn and the Calf
sum: The chapter opens with an alarm. A horn is raised, an eagle circles the LORD's house, and the charge is read: Israel has broken the covenant and rebelled against the law, while crying out 'We know you.' The rest names the sins in a list: kings made without the LORD, a calf made by a craftsman, pay given to foreign powers, altars built to cover sin, sacrifices that please no one, and fine houses built by a people who 'forgot his Maker'.

The chapter turns on one line, 'They sow wind, so a storm wind is what they will reap' (8:7). Sowing wind is hollow work, and the harvest is a storm. The chapter ends in exile, the Exodus run backwards: 'They will go back to Egypt.'
readings: Read as a warning to Samaria in its last decades

The kings who made themselves (8:4), the payments to Assyria (8:9) and the building boom (8:14) fit the years after Jeroboam II's death, when thrones were taken by force and the kingdom had to buy peace from Assyria.
Read as a charge-sheet in the form of a covenant lawsuit

The chapter is arranged as a list of broken covenant terms: the law (8:1, 12), the false worship (8:4-6, 11), the foreign alliances (8:8-10) and the empty offerings (8:13). The curse that closes it, 'back to Egypt', is the curse of Deuteronomy 28:68.

views.H: The eighth century northern kingdom after Jeroboam II (died about 753 BC): the rapid succession of kings (2 Kings 15), tribute to Tiglath-pileser III (2 Kings 15:19-20), the Syro-Ephraimite pressure and then Hoshea's appeal to Egypt (2 Kings 17:3-4). The fall of Samaria in 722 BC is the exile the chapter promises.
views.C: The chapter is full of hard Hebrew: the Ketiv and Qere at 8:12, the word that appears only once at 8:13, the unclear 'writhe' at 8:10, and the line about Judah at 8:14, which many scholars attribute to a Judean reader after 722. The mention of a written law at 8:12 is cited both for and against an early Pentateuch. Verses 8:1-3 may be an editor's heading to the whole group of oracles (chapters 8-10).
views.J: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak generally read Hosea as aimed at the northern kingdom and its calves, with the exile of the Ten Tribes as the result; they differ over many words in the chapter. No common haftarah is taken from this chapter. The alarm and the eagle are read as a warning of Assyria.
views.X: Christian readers, from the fathers to the Reformers, have read the chapter as a warning to the church as well as to Israel: the calf and the foreign alliances stand for whatever is trusted in place of God, and religious words without obedience ('we know you') are not enough. The line about sowing the wind has passed into daily speech as a proverb about sin and its results.
views.F: Most futurist readers see the chapter as fulfilled in the Assyrian conquest. The 'return to Egypt' and the 'house of the LORD' are sometimes linked by dispensational readers with the end-time distress of Israel, but the text names no end-time event.

deep.h: What 'calf' and 'idol' meant to the Israelites
deep.b: A common assumption is that the calf was a pagan idol. Many scholars think it was meant as a throne or pedestal for the invisible LORD, like the cherubim of the ark (Exodus 25:18-22). On that view, Jeroboam's calves were an alternate to Jerusalem's ark, not a rival god. Hosea will not allow the defense: 'A craftsman made it, and it is no god' (8:6). The point is that a thing made by hands cannot carry the LORD's presence, and the people's trust in it turned worship into a counterfeit.

For chapters 8-14 the Hebrew is the Leningrad Codex, the Greek is Swete's edition (from Codex Vaticanus), and the Dead Sea scrolls are read in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook. At 8:1 the scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves words from the first half of the verse and, in what it shows, agrees with the Masoretic Text. No scroll preserves the rest of the chapter. The Greek of 8:1 begins with a different word than the Hebrew, and in 8:5, 8:10 and 8:12 it reads a different pointing; the variants record the places where the sense changes.

traditions.q: Does God appoint every ruler? Hosea 8:4 has the LORD say of Israel's kings, 'the choice was not mine'. Hosea does not address government in general: the verse is about kings made without the LORD's approval. The card sets it beside Romans 13:1, which says the authorities are appointed by God.
views: Authority comes from God, but it binds only as it serves the common good; citizens owe obedience to legitimate rulers except where they command what is against the moral order, and a ruler who uses power unjustly loses his claim (Catechism 1897-1904, 2242).

The ideal is cooperation between church and ruler, and obedience to the state is a Christian duty, but it ends where the state demands that believers act against their faith (Russian Orthodox Church, Basis of the Social Concept, 2000).

Rulers are God's order for the world, and Christians may serve in office and obey, but when a command cannot be obeyed without sin 'we must obey God rather than men' (Augsburg Confession, article 16).

Civil magistrates are ordained by God for his glory and the public good (Westminster Confession 23.1); Calvin taught obedience even to poor rulers, except where they command what God forbids, and allowed lesser magistrates to restrain a tyrant (Institutes 4.20).

Government is 'ordained of God' as a sword outside the perfection of Christ; the Christian follows Christ's way of nonresistance and does not serve as a magistrate or bear the sword (Schleitheim Confession, article 6).

Government is ordained by God for human welfare and is to be obeyed in all things not contrary to the word of God; church and state are separate and conscience is free (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, articles XV and XVII).

echoes: Deuteronomy 28:68; Deuteronomy 31:9; 1 Kings 12:28-30; 2 Kings 15:10-30; 2 Kings 17:3-6; Isaiah 10:8; Jeremiah 22:28; Amos 2:5; Hosea 5:8; Hosea 9:3; Hosea 13:10-11

settings.what: A warning and a charge against the northern kingdom
settings.to: The people and rulers of the northern kingdom of Israel (Ephraim), with a word on Judah at the end (8:14)
settings.when: After Jeroboam II, in the years of rapid change of kings and of tribute to Assyria (about 750-725 BC)
settings.why: To sound an alarm: the covenant that Israel claims to know has been broken, and the things it relies on (kings, a calf, foreign powers, sacrifices, fortresses) will not save it. Knowing the audience changes the sense of 'we know you': it is the cry of people who think a few religious words will cover everything.
settings.readers: Hosea's words were kept after the northern kingdom fell, probably by people in Judah who saw in them their own story (8:14).
views: Many place it between 750 and 735 BC, in the turmoil after Jeroboam II (Menahem's tribute, 2 Kings 15:19-20).
Others set it later, between 732 and 725 BC, when Pekah had lost much of the land and Hoshea sought help from Egypt (2 Kings 17:3-4).

title: No Joy at the Harvest
sum: The chapter is spoken at a harvest feast. Everyone is glad about the grain and the wine, and the prophet says: do not rejoice. The crop is a payment from the gods of fertility, the land is the LORD's and will not be theirs for long, and the next feast will be held in Egypt or in Assyria, on unclean food. The prophet's own role is hard (9:7-9): they call him a fool, and set a trap on his path.

The second half looks back to the start and forward to the end. The LORD found Israel like grapes in the desert, and they went to Baal of Peor (9:10). From there the speech runs down to a single theme: no children. Ephraim, whose name means 'fruitful', will bear no fruit. The prophet asks for it (9:14), and the LORD says 'I will love them no more' (9:15). The book's hardest chapter ends in wandering.
readings: Read as a speech at the autumn harvest

The opening and the festival of 9:5 give a precise setting: the harvest gathering at a shrine of the northern kingdom, perhaps Bethel or Gilgal. The speech is aimed at the pilgrims and the priests who had come for the feast.
Read as a poem built on one name
The second half plays on the name Ephraim: the 'fruitful' one is struck, his root dries up, he has no fruit. The images of birth, womb, breast and conception are all the language of a name.

views.H: Spoken in the last years of the northern kingdom (about 740-725 BC), when Assyria was already taking land and some northerners had fled to Egypt. The prophet's sharp words are a reaction to the festival crowds, and the fate they describe (Egypt, Assyria, no children, wandering) was what Samaria's fall brought in 722 BC.
views.C: This is one of the hardest chapters in the book. Verses 9:7-9 are almost unreadable: who speaks, and who is the watchman? 9:13 has a damaged line. The chapter may combine a feast-day oracle (9:1-6), a reflection on the prophet's treatment (9:7-9) and a historical poem (9:10-17). The Greek is often different from the Hebrew, but it is also uncertain.
views.J: Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Radak read the chapter as aimed at the Ten Tribes and their pilgrimage feasts, with 'Egypt' and 'Assyria' as the places of exile. The mention of a prophet who is called mad is read as a statement of what the people say of any true prophet. Nothing in the chapter is used as a haftarah in the standard customs.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in 9:7 the rejection of the prophets, taken up in the Gospels (Matthew 23:37; Acts 7:52). Jesus' words on the road to the cross (Luke 23:29-30) echo 9:14 and 10:8.
views.F: Most futurist readers treat the chapter as fulfilled in 722 BC. A few link the 'wandering among the nations' (9:17) with the dispersion of the Jewish people and the return promised later in the book (11:10-11; 14:4-7).

deep.b: The great autumn feast, later called Booths, ended the farming year. It was glad: the vineyards had been picked, the grain gathered, and Israel was told to rejoice before the LORD (Deuteronomy 16:13-15). Hosea says the joy has a rotten root. To the farmers of Canaan a good harvest meant that Baal, the storm god, had been paid his due; the prophet says the grain is a gift of the LORD (2:8) and that those who credit another god for it are being fed by a counterfeit. The same set of ideas lies behind 13:6, where the LORD says that the people were filled and forgot him.

In this chapter 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves parts of 9:1-4 and 9:9-17, with many words restored by the editors. It agrees with the Masoretic Text in the words it preserves. The Greek often differs: at 9:2 it says the winepress 'did not know' them; at 9:7 it makes the prophet one who 'is beside himself'; at 9:13 it reads 'for the hunt' (see the variant). The Qere in 9:16 is spelling only.

echoes: Deuteronomy 16:13-15; Deuteronomy 23:18; Numbers 25:1-3; Judges 19:30; Ezekiel 4:13; Jeremiah 2:2-3; Luke 23:29-30; 2 Kings 9:11; Genesis 41:52

settings.what: A warning at the harvest feast
settings.to: The pilgrims and priests gathered for the autumn feast at a northern shrine (Bethel or Gilgal)
settings.when: At the harvest feast, in the last decades of the kingdom (about 740-725 BC)
settings.why: To turn the festival's joy to mourning: the harvest is not a gift of Baal, the land is the LORD's and will be lost, and the prophet who says so will be mocked. Knowing the setting explains why the opening is a command not to rejoice, and why the prophet answers the crowd who call him mad.
settings.readers: Later readers, in Judah and in exile, would have read the chapter as a description of what had happened and as a warning for their own harvest.
views: Many commentators picture an actual speech at the festival.
Others think the festival is a frame set by the writer for a collection of sayings from various times.

settings.what: The LORD's look back and the curse of childlessness
settings.by: The LORD, with the prophet's prayer in 9:14
settings.to: The people of Ephraim and, through them, the whole nation
settings.when: The same period; the look back is on the whole of Israel's history from the wilderness to the present
settings.why: To show that Israel's apostasy is old (Baal of Peor), that it has deep roots (Gilgal, Gibeah), and that the loss of every child is the result. The word to Ephraim is also a word about the nation's future: no sons means no future.

title: A Luxuriant Vine
sum: The chapter begins with a vine and ends with a king cut off at dawn. Israel is a luxuriant vine that bore fruit for itself, and the more it prospered the more altars and pillars it built. The LORD will break the altars like the necks of animals, and the king will drift like a twig. The calf of Beth-aven will go to Assyria as tribute (10:5-6), and the people will cry to the mountains, 'Cover us!' (10:8).

In the middle comes a call (10:12): sow righteousness, reap by the measure of loyal love, plow new ground, seek the LORD until he comes and rains righteousness on you. Then the speech turns back to what they did instead: they plowed wickedness and reaped injustice, and trusted in their own way and in their army (10:13). Bethel will do it to them, and the king of Israel will be cut off.
readings: Read as the end of a country's story
The chapter looks back from the edge of exile: a prosperous nation, rich shrines, a crumbling throne, the calf in Assyrian hands and the king gone. The call of 10:12 is the last offer.
Read as a farming parable

The whole chapter is built on the farm: vine, fruit, furrows, poison weed, heifer, yoke, plow, harrow, sow, reap. Each section answers the one before: Israel's fruit became altars; its yoke becomes real labor; its sown wickedness yields injustice.

views.H: Spoken in the last years of Samaria (about 735-725 BC): the 'no king' of 10:3 fits the years after Hoshea's arrest (2 Kings 17:4), and the calf carried to Assyria fits the practice recorded in Assyrian inscriptions. Gibeah (10:9) was Saul's town, so that verse may also touch on the first king.
views.C: The chapter is dense with hard words: boqeq (10:1), the Ketiv-Qere at 10:10, Shalman and Beth-arbel (10:14). The Greek differs at 10:1, 10:5, 10:12 and 10:14. Some critics find the Jacob-Judah line in 10:11 a Judean addition, and a few see 10:12 as an editor's call to repent added to a gloomy oracle.
views.J: The Targum, Rashi and Radak read the chapter as a rebuke to the northern tribes for their altars and calves. Hosea 10:12 ('sow for yourselves in righteousness') is taken as a call to repentance. The verse about the cry to the mountains is read as the terror of invasion.
views.X: Christian readers have always read 10:8 with Luke 23:30 and Revelation 6:16: what Hosea said of Samaria's fall, Jesus said of Jerusalem's, and John of the end. The vine of 10:1 is set beside Jesus' 'I am the true vine' (John 15:1). Jerome's Latin renders the Hebrew 'mouth' of 10:12 literally ('reap in the mouth of mercy') and has 'renew your fallow ground' for 'plow new ground'. (The King James Version's 'break up your fallow ground' is the form preachers made famous.)
views.F: Some futurist readers see in 10:8 the same distress as Revelation 6:16 and treat Hosea's words as a sign of the end. Most take the chapter as fulfilled in 722 BC and the call of 10:12 as open to every generation.

deep.b: The picture in 10:11 depends on how an ox was used. In the threshing yard an ox walked round and round on the sheaves, dragging a sledge, and was allowed to eat the grain as it went (Deuteronomy 25:4). In the field the same ox was yoked and made to plow. Hosea says that the LORD spared Ephraim's neck, but now there is a new season: Ephraim will pull, Judah will plow, Jacob will harrow. Jeremiah borrows the picture when Ephraim says he was "like a calf that was never trained" (Jeremiah 31:18). It is a picture of discipline after ease.

The scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves much of chapter 10. It reads clearly, with nothing restored, through most of 10:1, 10:4, 10:6, 10:9 and 10:11, the first words of 10:2, the word qetsef in 10:7, and parts of 10:5, 10:12, 10:13 and 10:15; words are heavily restored at 10:3, 10:8, 10:10 and 10:14. Where it can be read it agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling (for example it writes the verb of 10:2 with a full vowel), including 'King Jareb' (10:6) and 'Judah will plow' (10:11). The Greek has several differences that matter: 10:1 'fruitful vine', 10:5 'calf of the house of On', 10:6 'Iareim', 10:10 and the Ketiv-Qere, 10:11 'I will keep silent about Judah', 10:12 'harvest the fruit of life', 10:14 'from the house of Jeroboam'. The last words of the Hebrew 10:15 stand at the start of the Greek chapter 11.

echoes: Psalm 80:8-16; Isaiah 5:1-7; Jeremiah 2:21; Jeremiah 31:18; Amos 6:12; Luke 23:30; Revelation 6:16; Judges 19-21; 1 Kings 12:29; John 15:1

settings.what: A judgment oracle on the shrines and the throne
settings.to: The northern kingdom's people, priests and rulers, in a time of prosperity and then of decline
settings.when: In the last decades of Samaria (about 740-725 BC), after kings had been made and unmade
settings.why: To say that the prosperity was spent on altars, not on justice; that the king they trust will fall; and that the calf they trust will be carried off. To the first hearers the calf was their safeguard; the oracle says it is a hostage.
settings.readers: Readers after 722 saw it as a record of the fall and of the cult's failure.

settings.what: The heifer, the call to sow righteousness, and the end of the king
settings.to: Ephraim, Judah and Jacob (the whole people), and by name Bethel
settings.why: To say that the LORD has trained Ephraim and now sets new work; to call the hearers to seek him while he can still be found; and to warn that Bethel (the shrine they trust) will be their undoing. The call of 10:12 is the only way out the chapter gives.

title: A Boy Called Out of Egypt
sum: The center of Hosea is a parent's speech. When Israel was a young boy the LORD loved him, called him out of Egypt, taught him to walk, held him by the arms, and lifted the yoke so he could eat. But the more the LORD called, the more the child walked away to the Baals. So the sword will come, and Assyria will rule (11:5-7).

Then comes the turn: 'How can I give you away, Ephraim?' The LORD's heart turns over inside him like the cities of the plain, Admah and Zeboiim, overturned for their sin. He will not act on the heat of his anger, because he is God and not a human being. The lion will roar, not against his children but to call them home from Egypt and Assyria. The last verse (11:12, Hebrew 12:1) goes back to Ephraim's lies and Judah's wandering, a sign that the chapter's love does not cancel the charge.
readings: Read as a family story
The chapter is a parent's memory in five scenes: the call, the walking lesson, the yoke eased, the child's flight and the parent's decision. The language is about a household, not a court.
Read as the answer to the lawsuit

Chapters 4-10 charge Ephraim; chapter 11 shows what the LORD does with the verdict. He says the punishment must come (11:5-6) and also says he will not finish it (11:8-9). The two stand side by side without being reconciled in the text.

views.H: A reflection from the last years of the northern kingdom (about 735-725 BC): Israel's history from the Exodus to Assyria's rule (11:5). It looks back at the Exodus and the wilderness, forward to a return from 'Egypt' and 'Assyria' that the eighth-century hearer could not yet see.
views.C: 11:1-11 is widely taken as the high point of the book's theology. Some critics treat 11:10-11 as a later hope added after 722 (the exile was already past when the return is described), and 11:12 (Hebrew 12:1) as the start of the next unit. The Greek differs at 11:1 (his children), 11:2, 11:3, 11:5 and 11:12.
views.J: Jewish tradition keeps Hosea 11:1-8 close to the story of the Exodus: the people are God's firstborn son. The haftarah for the Sabbath of Vayetzei (the Jacob reading in Genesis) comes from Hosea: Sephardic custom reads Hosea 11:7 to 12:12 in the Hebrew numbering (English 11:7 to 12:11), and Ashkenazic custom reads Hebrew 12:13 to 14:10 (English 12:12 to 14:9), so the Jacob chapter is heard beside Genesis. In modern Jewish thought, Abraham Joshua Heschel built his account of divine 'pathos' on chapters like this one.
views.X: Christian readers hear Matthew 2:15 in 11:1: Jesus is the true Son who goes down to Egypt and comes out. Jerome noted that the Hebrew has 'my son' and the Greek 'his children'. The turn at 11:8 has been read as a window into the heart of God that is opened wide in the cross. Church writers differ on how far it describes God's feeling (see the card).
views.F: Futurist readers take 11:10-11 as a promise of Israel's regathering from Egypt and Assyria and read it with the return passages in Isaiah and Ezekiel; others read it as fulfilled in the return from Babylon and in the church. Romans 11 is often joined with it.

deep.b: The chapter is the Exodus retold as a parent's story. Exodus 4:22-23 had called Israel "my son" and demanded Pharaoh let him go. Deuteronomy 1:31 said the LORD carried Israel like a son. Hosea adds the details a parent would remember: the first steps, the arms, the healing, the yoke eased, the food held out. The tone of the chapter is grief more than anger. Because the speaker is the LORD, the language of change ("my heart turns over") is the book's most direct picture of how God relates to a people that refuses him.

deep.h: The Greek and the scrolls in this chapter
deep.b: The Greek has several places where it differs from the Hebrew in this chapter: "his children" (11:1), "I called" (11:2), "I shackled" (11:3), "lived in Egypt" (11:5), and a different last verse (11:12). In 11:8 it reads "how shall I set you, Ephraim, protect you, Israel?" and "my repentance (metameleia) was stirred". 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves most of 11:1-12 in part, with restorations. In the words that are visible it agrees with the Masoretic Text (spelling aside), with one candidate difference at 11:10, where it appears to have a singular verb ("he will walk") for the Masoretic plural ("they will walk"). That reading depends on a transcription whose neighbors are restored, so the Plain does not use it.

echoes: Exodus 4:22-23; Deuteronomy 1:31; Deuteronomy 29:23; Genesis 19:25; Jeremiah 31:9; Jeremiah 31:20; Amos 1:2; Matthew 2:15; Hosea 5:14; Hosea 13:7; Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29

settings.what: The LORD's reflection on his son Ephraim
settings.by: The LORD, through Hosea, speaking as a parent
settings.to: The people of Ephraim, and through them all Israel
settings.when: In the last years of the northern kingdom, after the verdicts of chapters 4-10
settings.why: To show the people who it is they have been rejecting: not a distant judge but a parent who raised them. The speech does not cancel the sentence of 11:5-7; it shows that the LORD will not let anger finish the story. For hearers who thought God's anger was the end, it opened the possibility of a future.
settings.readers: For the readers after 722, living with the exile, 11:8-11 is the ground of the hope that the LORD will bring his children home.
views: Many read 11:1-11 as one speech with a turning point at 11:8.
Others find a judgment oracle (11:1-7) and a later promise (11:8-11) joined by an editor.

settings.what: The LORD's case against Ephraim and Judah, told with Jacob's story
settings.why: To bring a covenant charge against both kingdoms, taking Jacob, the ancestor of both, as the pattern of their ways. The speech turns on the point that the people have become what their ancestor was at his worst (the deceiver), when they were meant to become what he was at his best (the one who wept and sought God).

traditions.q: Matthew says Hosea 11:1 was 'fulfilled' in Jesus, though Hosea was speaking of the Exodus. How can that be?
views: Scripture has a literal sense and spiritual senses based on it; the allegorical or typological sense sees in persons and events of the Old Testament a pattern fulfilled in Christ, so the Exodus pattern is completed in him (Catechism 115-117, 128-130; Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 10).

The Fathers read the Old Testament as spoken by the same Spirit who spoke in the Gospels, with events such as the Exodus carrying a meaning that is fully seen in Christ; Matthew's quotation is an example of the apostolic reading that the church follows (John Chrysostom, Homilies on Matthew).

Christ is the center of the whole Bible. Luther called the Old Testament the swaddling clothes and the manger in which Christ lies, and Lutheran teaching reads Matthew's use of Hosea in that light (Luther, Preface to the Old Testament).

Calvin held that the church's deliverance from Egypt is renewed in Christ, its Head, so Matthew rightly applies what was said of the body to the head; he opposed allegories that find hidden meanings beyond the plain sense of the text (Commentary on a Harmony of the Evangelists, on Matthew 2:15; lectures on Hosea 11:1).
Some dispensational writers, for example John Walvoord (Matthew: Thy Kingdom Come), hold that Hosea 11:1 is about the historic Exodus and treat Matthew's use as an application or parallel.

traditions.q: Does God feel pain and change his mind, as Hosea 11:8-9 seems to say, or is that a human way of speaking about him?
views: God is unchanging and without passions in his being; words like grief and pity are said of God by analogy, for the effects of love, not as feelings that happen to him (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 21, a. 3). His love is real, shown above all in the cross.

God is unchanging in his being, but not remote: the Son, who is God, suffered in the flesh, and the church sings of 'God crucified for us'. Hosea's words are heard in the light of that (Ware, The Orthodox Church).

God is 'without body, parts, or passions, immutable' (Westminster Confession 2.1). Scripture speaks to us in human terms; Calvin calls this God's accommodation to our weakness, as when it says God 'repents' (Institutes 1.17.12-13).

The Lutheran confessions do not address divine impassibility directly. They teach that the one person of Christ is both God and man, and that what is said of either nature is said of the person (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration 8); the Lutheran Old Testament scholar Terence Fretheim reads Hosea 11 as showing that God really suffers with his people.

Evangelicals are divided. Many hold the classical doctrine that God does not change in character or purpose, and read the language as accommodation; the 'openness of God' view (Clark Pinnock, John Sanders and others) holds that God really responds in time and that Hosea 11 shows it.

title: Jacob and Ephraim
sum: The chapter opens with Ephraim's foreign policy as wind-herding: a covenant with Assyria in one hand, oil sent to Egypt in the other. Then the LORD brings a case, and the evidence is Jacob. In the womb he grabbed his brother's heel; as a man he struggled with God; he wept and begged; at Bethel God spoke with him, and with 'us'. From this the prophet speaks: 'But you must turn back to your God. Keep loyal love and justice, and keep waiting for your God, always.'

The second half is a series of contrasts. Canaan has rigged scales (12:7). Ephraim says he is rich and clean (12:8). The LORD has been his God since Egypt and sent prophets (12:9-10). Gilead and Gilgal have altars like piles of stones (12:11). Jacob fled to Aram and served for a wife; the LORD brought Israel out of Egypt by a prophet (12:12-13). The chapter ends with Ephraim's bitter provocation and the blood guilt left on him.
readings: Read as a hostile reading of Jacob
Each detail of Jacob's story is a fault: the heel-grabber, the schemer who wrestles for a blessing, the servant who fled. The people have the ancestor's nature and the same punishment.
Read as a hopeful reading of Jacob
The same details are Jacob at his best: persistent, struggling with God, weeping, answered at Bethel. The people are told to be what he became, and the call of 12:6 is the application.

views.H: Spoken against the diplomacy of the last years of Samaria: tribute to Assyria and gifts to Egypt (12:1; 2 Kings 17:3-4), the trade and wealth of the kingdom under Jeroboam II (12:7-8), and the shrines at Gilgal and Gilead (12:11). The Jacob material matches the northern kingdom's own claim on the patriarch.
views.C: The chapter is one of the hardest in the book. Verses 12:3-6 are read by some as an original northern Jacob tradition and by others as a post-722 Judean rewrite (12:2 includes Judah). The Hebrew has a rare verb in 12:10, two hard readings in 12:4 and the Greek has many differences. The numbering shift (English 12:1 is Hebrew 12:2) is only a matter of versification.
views.J: The chapter is read in the synagogue beside Genesis: the haftarah for Vayetzei, the portion in which Jacob flees to Aram, draws on Hosea 11-14: Sephardic custom reads Hosea 11:7 to 12:12 in the Hebrew numbering (English 11:7 to 12:11), and Ashkenazic custom reads Hebrew 12:13 to 14:10 (English 12:12 to 14:9). Jewish commentators generally take verses 3-6 as holding up Jacob's tears and prayer as the model for his descendants, and read verse 6 as the call to teshuvah (return). The identification of the 'angel' follows the Jewish debate on Genesis 32.
views.X: Christian readers have heard in Hosea's 'angel' and 'God' the voice of the pre-incarnate Son in some of the fathers' reading of Genesis 32. The call to 'turn back to your God' is a main text for repentance in Reformation preaching. The two accounts of Jacob (heel-grabber, then Israel) became a Christian picture of the old and new self.
views.F: Futurist readers see the tents of 12:9 as a promise tied to the future feast of Booths (Zechariah 14:16) or as a sign of Israel's restoration; others treat it as fulfilled in the return from exile. The chapter's call to turn back (12:6) is read as the pattern for national repentance.

deep.b: Hosea names Jacob in 10:11, 12:2 and 12:12 and uses "Israel" for the man in 12:12-13. In the first part of the chapter Jacob is the shared father of both kingdoms. The prophet tells his story in three Genesis scenes: the birth (Genesis 25:26), the night at the river (Genesis 32), and the vision at Bethel (Genesis 28; 35). Whether he is held up as warning, example or both is debated. A path through the debate: the same traits that were Jacob's fault (grasping, striving) are also his strength when turned toward God, and Hosea invites his descendants to use them that way.

English 11:12 is Hebrew 12:1, and English 12:1-14 are Hebrew 12:2-15. The Greek keeps the English divisions here. The Dead Sea scroll 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves parts of most verses of 12:1-14, with many words restored. Where it can be read it agrees with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling and the possible omission noted at 12:1. The Greek differs at 12:1 ('an evil spirit', 'he increased empty and vain things'), 12:4, 12:7 ('Canaan: a yoke of injustice is in his hand'), 12:10 ('I was made like') and 12:11 (Gilead twice, 'rulers' for 'bulls', 'turtles' for 'heaps'; 4QXIIg preserves 'in Gilgal they sacrifice bulls' unrestored, as the Masoretic Text has it).

echoes: Genesis 25:26; Genesis 27:36; Genesis 28:10-22; Genesis 32:22-32; Genesis 35:1-15; Exodus 3:15; Leviticus 23:42-43; Deuteronomy 18:15; Deuteronomy 26:5; Ezekiel 16:3; Amos 8:5; Revelation 3:17

settings.what: The LORD's recital of what he has done, and the verdict
settings.to: Ephraim and the people of the northern kingdom, in the voice of one who has been betrayed
settings.when: The same period, in the last years of Samaria
settings.why: To remind a rich and self-satisfied people that the LORD has been their God since Egypt, that he sent prophets, and that they have turned away. The recital turns the claim of 12:8 ('no guilt in me') around: the LORD's record of care is the proof of Ephraim's guilt.
settings.readers: For readers after 722, the chapter was both an explanation of the fall and a call to learn from Jacob.

title: Death, Where Are Your Plagues?
sum: The chapter runs from Ephraim's rise to his death. Ephraim spoke and Israel shuddered, but he fell into guilt through Baal and died (13:1). Now they make silver calves and say 'kiss calves' (13:2). So they will be mist, dew, chaff, smoke (13:3). The LORD recalls that he has been their God since Egypt, and knew them in the desert; they were fed, and forgot him (13:4-6). So he will be a lion, a leopard, a bear (13:7-8). Where is the king they asked for? He was given in anger (13:10-11).

Then comes the verse that Paul reached for: 'Should I ransom them from the hand of Sheol? ... Where are your plagues, Death?' (13:14). Whether the lines promise or threaten is one of the oldest questions in the book. The chapter ends with the wind of the LORD drying up Ephraim's spring and the fall of Samaria described without softening: 'they will fall by the sword' (13:16).
readings: Read as a threat

Death and Sheol are called up as the LORD's servants. The questions ('Should I ransom them?') expect the answer no, the last line ('Pity is hidden from my eyes') closes the door, and the chapter ends in war.
Read as a promise

The LORD defies Death, and the questions are rhetorical challenges. The reading underlies Paul's use in 1 Corinthians 15:55 and the Latin and Greek Christian tradition, and in a book that ends with 'I will heal their turning away' (14:4) it is not out of place.

views.H: Spoken in the last years of Samaria (about 730-725 BC). The kings (13:10-11) are the usurpers of 2 Kings 15 and Hoshea; the 'wind from the wilderness' is the Assyrian invasion; 13:16 foretells the siege and the sack of 722 BC. The Hebrew of 13:14 may be an ironic summons: Death, do your work on Ephraim.
views.C: A very hard chapter. 13:1 and 13:14 are both unclear. The Greek differs at 13:1, 13:2, 13:4 (a long plus, also in 4QXIIc), 13:7 and 13:14. Some critics find 13:14 out of place and a later hopeful addition; others find it central. Many hold 13:10-11 to be the voice of a prophet who opposed the monarchy; others, a Judean reading of the north's kings. The versification shift at 13:16 is an artefact of the Hebrew chapter division.
views.J: Jewish commentators have read 13:14 both as a question expecting 'no' and as a promise of rescue. The chapter is heard in the synagogue in the Ashkenazic haftarah for Vayetzei, which starts at Hosea 12:13 (Hebrew numbering) and runs through chapter 13 into chapter 14. The 'kissing calves' of 13:2 is read by Rashi and Radak as the people's homage to Jeroboam's calves.
views.X: Christian readers hear Paul's victory song in 13:14: 'Where, Death, is your victory? Where, Death, is your sting?' (1 Corinthians 15:55). Jerome's Latin put it as a promise ('O death, I will be your death'), and Luther's German Bible does the same. The Greek 'Hades' reading lies behind the Easter hymns of the East. Many modern Christian commentators see a threat in the Hebrew and a reuse by Paul.
views.F: Futurist readers take 13:14 with 1 Corinthians 15 as a promise for the resurrection at the end (and some with 6:2, the third day). The 'wind of the LORD' is sometimes taken as a type of the invasion of the end-time. Most hold that 13:15-16 were fulfilled in 722 BC.

deep.b: Paul does not name Hosea in 1 Corinthians 15:55 and may be drawing on the Greek text as he knew it. Three questions are asked of the use. (1) Does Paul use the verse in its original sense? If Hosea meant a threat, Paul reverses it: the answer to "Where is your sting?" is no longer "Come, bring it" but "nowhere". If Hosea meant a promise, Paul follows it. (2) Does Paul quote the Greek or the Hebrew? He is nearer the Greek ("sting", "Death" addressed twice), but he changes it. (3) Does the Hebrew's final line ("Pity is hidden") matter? Paul omits it. The card on this verse sets out how the churches have answered.

For this chapter two Dead Sea scrolls are read in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook. 4QXIIc (4Q78) preserves parts of 13:3-10 and 13:15-16, the end of the chapter, with a long plus at 13:4 and the reading 'of the forest' at 13:8. 4QXIIg (4Q82) preserves parts of 13:1, 13:7-8 and 13:11-13, with many words restored (13:6 is only one restored word). They agree with the Masoretic Text apart from spelling, except at 13:4 and 13:8; at 13:5 4QXIIc preserves 'I knew you', against the Greek 'I shepherded you'. At 13:10 4QXIIc writes the word for 'where' as 'ayyeh where the Masoretic Text has 'ehi; the Greek and the Latin also read 'where' at 13:10. At 13:14, which neither scroll preserves, the Latin reads the same Masoretic spelling as 'I will be'. The Greek differs in many places (13:1, 13:2, 13:4, 13:5, 13:7, 13:9, 13:13, 13:14).

echoes: Deuteronomy 8:14; Deuteronomy 32:15; Deuteronomy 32:34; 1 Samuel 8:5; 1 Samuel 9:16; 1 Kings 19:18; Exodus 14:21; Psalm 49:15; Isaiah 25:8; Amos 3:2; 2 Kings 15:16; 1 Corinthians 15:55

settings.what: The last charge against Ephraim: from rise to fall
settings.to: The people of Ephraim, and their king, in the last years of the northern kingdom
settings.when: About 730-725 BC, as Assyria closes in (and perhaps in the weeks before Samaria's siege, 725-722 BC)
settings.why: To show that the end is no surprise: Ephraim's history is told in a few lines, from the day he was exalted to the day he 'died', and each stage points to the next. The LORD recalls his own care (13:4-6) so that the people will see their forgetting, and he names the end plainly. For hearers who trusted in the king and the calves, the chapter says both are useless.
settings.readers: After 722 the chapter was read as the explanation of the fall and, through 13:14, as a text to hold against death in later centuries.
views: Many place 13:1-16 near the end of Hosea's ministry (the king 'taken away' may be Hoshea's capture in 724).
Others find several oracles joined by catchwords: wind and dew (13:3, 15), Egypt (13:4), king (13:10-11).

traditions.q: Does Hosea 13:14 promise victory over death or threaten death, and is Paul using it in its own sense?
views: Jerome's Vulgate reads it as a promise of victory ('O death, I will be your death; O hell, I will be your bite'), which depends on reading the Hebrew word 'ehi as 'I will be'; the church has read it with 1 Corinthians 15:55 as Christ's victory over death. Medieval Roman chant books give the Latin words as an antiphon for Holy Saturday (not checked against the present Liturgy of the Hours).

The Greek form of the verse, the Old Testament text of the Greek-speaking church, reads the lines as a promise ('I will ransom them from the hand of Hades'). The paschal homily attributed to John Chrysostom, read at the Easter service, sings Paul's version of the question from 1 Corinthians 15:55: 'Where, O Death, is your sting? Where, O Hades, is your victory?' It draws on Paul and does not discuss the Hebrew.

Luther's German Bible renders the lines as a promise: 'I will ransom them from hell and rescue them from death. Death, I will be a poison to you; hell, I will be a plague to you.' Lutheran preaching uses it with Paul in the Easter and funeral liturgy.

Calvin, lecturing on Hosea 13:14, reads the lines as conditional: the LORD would be Israel's redeemer, but the people's obstinacy blocks the grace he offers, so the verse belongs to the threat around it. He argues against taking it as an unconditional promise (Calvin, lectures on the Twelve Minor Prophets).
E. B. Pusey's commentary on the Minor Prophets reads the verse as a promise fulfilled in Christ's resurrection, and the Prayer Book funeral service carries Paul's words from 1 Corinthians 15.

Evangelical commentaries are divided. Some read the Hebrew as the LORD's challenge to death and so a promise; others read it as a threat in Hosea's own setting that Paul takes up in a new sense, as the church's victory song.

title: Turn Back
sum: The book's last chapter is an invitation and an answer. 'Turn back, Israel, to the LORD your God, for you have stumbled over your guilt.' The prophet gives the people the words to say: 'Forgive all our guilt and accept what is good, and let us pay you the bulls of our lips. Assyria cannot save us. We will not ride on horses. We will no longer call the work of our hands "Our gods!" For in you the child with no father is shown compassion.'

The LORD answers with a string of promises: 'I will heal their turning away. I will love them freely.' He will be like the dew, and Israel will bloom like a lily, strike roots like Lebanon, and spread like an olive and a vine. The LORD is a cypress whose fruit is Ephraim's. The final verse steps out of the voice of the LORD to ask who is wise enough to understand, and tells the reader that the LORD's ways are straight: the righteous walk on them, and rebels stumble.
readings: Read as an offer made in time
Hosea sets out a way back, with prayer words ready to use, before the fall. It was a real offer to the northern kingdom, and the book's last word is that it could still turn.
Read as a hope after the fall

The chapter comes at the end of a book that has told the fall of Samaria in detail. It is the answer of the survivors: turn, be healed, grow. The final wisdom note tells later readers how to read what came before.

views.H: The call to turn back and the words to say fit the last years of Samaria, when Assyria and Egypt were the only hope the kings could see (14:3). Whether the chapter was spoken before the fall or put together afterward for the survivors, it is the book's plain statement of what the LORD wanted: not a better treaty but a changed people.
views.C: Many scholars read 14:1-8 as authentic, and 14:9 as a later wisdom note; some find the hopeful promises of 14:4-8 as post-722. The Hebrew text has problems at 14:2 ('bulls' or 'fruit'), 14:3 ('shown compassion'), 14:8 (the speaker; the Greek has 'humbled'). The Greek is close to the Hebrew in this chapter apart from these. The chapter divisions differ: English 14:1-9 is Hebrew 14:2-10.
views.J: Hosea 14:2-10 (Hebrew numbering) is the reading for the Sabbath of Return (Shabbat Shuvah) before the Day of Atonement, and ends the haftarah for Vayetzei in the Ashkenazic custom. The Talmud draws on 14:1 for its teaching that repentance turns willful sin into error (Yoma 86b). 'The bulls of our lips' became the rabbinic ground for prayer in place of sacrifice.
views.X: Hebrews 13:15 follows the Greek of 14:2: 'the fruit of lips that confess his name.' The Roman lectionary reads Hosea 14:2-10 (Hebrew numbering; English 14:1-9) as the first reading for the Friday of the Third Week of Lent. Christian readers have heard in 14:4 the grace that comes before the turning, and in 14:9 a closing call to wisdom. Many see the 'fatherless' of 14:3 as the church's own place before the Father.
views.F: Futurist readers link 14:4-8 with the promises of Israel's restoration, along with Romans 11:26 ('and so all Israel will be saved'). Others take the chapter as realized in the return from Babylon, in the church, or in both.

deep.h: Prayer in place of the sacrifice
deep.b: Hosea 14:2-3 gives the people a script: what to bring (words), what to ask (forgiveness; acceptance of what is good), what to pledge (the sacrifice of lips) and what to renounce (Assyria, horses, idols). It is the most complete prayer of repentance in the prophets. The Hebrew "bulls of our lips" has been used for three thousand years to justify prayer in place of Temple offerings, in Judaism after AD 70 and in the church. The Greek "fruit of our lips" is the form Hebrews 13:15 knows.

For this chapter the scroll 4QXIIc (4Q78) preserves parts of 14:1-5, with several restorations, and 4QXIIg (4Q82) parts of 14:8-9. In 14:2 the scroll 4QXIIc has a doubled word for 'with you' (a copyist's slip) and its word for 'bulls' is restored; in 14:3 its verb 'is shown compassion' is spelled with a full vowel, the same word. In 14:4 4QXIIc preserves 'their turning away' unrestored. The Greek differs at 14:2 (fruit), 14:4 ('I will heal their dwellings'), 14:8 (humbled) and in the verse numbers: its 14:1 is the Hebrew 13:16, so the Greek chapter has ten verses.

echoes: Jeremiah 3:12; Jeremiah 3:22; Hosea 1:6; Hosea 2:23; Deuteronomy 17:16; Isaiah 31:1; Psalm 51:17; Psalm 107:43; Hebrews 13:15; Romans 11:26

settings.what: A call to turn back, the words to say, and the LORD's promise
settings.by: Hosea, then the LORD (the people's prayer is in the prophet's mouth)
settings.to: The people of Israel (Ephraim), in the days when Assyria and Egypt seemed the only hope
settings.when: Probably the last years of the northern kingdom; some think the chapter was shaped after 722 for the survivors
settings.why: To give the people a way out and the words to use. The prophet scripts their prayer so that none can say they did not know what to say; then the LORD answers for himself and shows what repentance leads to. To people who thought the end was certain, it says that the door is open.
settings.readers: Readers after the exile used it as the pattern of confession and the ground of hope; the synagogue still reads it before the Day of Atonement.
views: Many hold the call was spoken as Samaria faced Assyria.
Others hold the chapter was shaped for the survivors in Judah, and that the promises of 14:4-8 are a later hope.

settings.by: The writer or an editor of the book, in the manner of a wisdom teacher
settings.to: The reader of the book: the hearer who wants to understand
settings.when: At the close of the book, perhaps added after the fall of Samaria
settings.why: To tell the reader how to read the whole: the book's pictures are hard but the road they point to is straight, and the choice is between walking it and stumbling.
